6756:
My perspective is that it was competitive with many of the toggle switch and
hex pad-based S-100 systems of the day and systems like the Heathkit H8 in
terms of interface, though of course by then the market was already shifting
to standard keyboards. Really all it would have needed was a decent keyboard
and it could have at least been a good entry level computer (particularly
since it offered color and sound - something many regular computers didn't
have), even if it couldn't compete on RAM.  Of course the ideal would have
been a combo keyboard/RAM add-on as was mentioned.  Even bringing it to just
8K RAM and having a decent keyboard would have kept it competitive into the
early 1980's.
 
Of course, history tells us that computer conversions or add-ons were never
successful, be it the APF M/MP1000/Imagination Machine, the Mattel Keyboard
Component/ECS for the Intellivision and the Adam expansion module for the
ColecoVision (though of course that benefited from also being sold as a
stand alone machine). The Imagination Machine was the only one to make it
out by 1979 and the market might have been rather more receptive to
something like that since it was still taking shape.  Still, Bally's
distribution and advertising was hardly much better than what APF was
dealing with so it would have likely failed anyway.

6758:
Well, the original Keyboard Component for the Intellivision was actually
quite cool, so you should check that out, but they couldn't get the cost
down to make it a practical mass production item (something like 4,000 were
released, with many eventually recalled).  The ECS was/is obviously rather
crippled, especially in comparison. It is neat though how the ECS adds two
extra controller ports and three more channels of sound, totalling six.  In
fact some modern homebrews take advantage of all six sound channels if you
have an ECS.
 
I'm actually a big fan of the Coleco Adam, despite the power supply being in
the printer (I've since gotten an modded external supply). It was a great
architecture hampered by unreliable data (tape) drives and the
aforementioned printer. Certainly its future potential was demonstrated in
what became the MSX standard.

Some of the comments were a bit terse [so I added to them a little.]
Nothing in there or the Dave Nutting Manual about using vbTIMB as
anything other than a Time Base.

Most of the newer stuff I gleaned from the HVGLIB.H (which was in the
D.N.A. Manual as BALLYEQU.H) and thus is more descriptive than just
plugging numbers in...

There is a location in Magic Memory set aside for writing to to clear
out the Pixel Shifter before using it named WASTE at $0FFF (also called
WASTER), but the address that that affects at $4FFF didn't have a name,
though I did hear it referred to as "the Urinal" a few times.
When setting the Stack Pointer it's best to get it as far above the
display screen as possible, either at BEGRAM or higher.  If you are not
going to be using the Music CPU routines you can move it up to CT0, and
if you are not using SENTRY or the built-in interrupt handler you can
move it up higher.  I moved it all the way up to $5000 (SP decrements by
2 before PUSHing a word), hence the penciled-in note at a later date.

Setting bits is done by noting "2 to the power of ..." and then the bit
number 0 to 7.  Since the assembler doesn't understand that you can left
shift a '1' up into position using "1 << PSWZRO" for instance, is bit
number 6 and equates to 01000000B which you can use to mask off the Zero
Flag.  "1 << PSWCY" is bit 0 so there is no actual shift, just
00000001B, but if you know the abbreviations then that says Carry Flag
without having to write that as a comment.
Adding two bits together using '|' or just saying 'or' confuses the
assembler since it tries to do the OR first and then the shifts, so you
have to say "(1 << PSWCY) | (1 << PSWZRO)" using parenthesis, and that
is MUCH clearer than just putting a "65", a "$41" or even a "01000001B".
It all ends up getting compiled to the same thing.
Other equates in there are System Variable names, Music Note names, UPI
calls and macros.  And you can just use the PORT names and bit number
equates as in "IN A,(SW0)"; "BIT CHTRIG,A" and not have to explain that
that is set on the Trigger pulled on Joystick One, although I would add
the comment anyway.

As you can see in the original version, nothing is drawn until the
joystick is moved, when the directional mask is translated by MSKTD into
movement deltas and stored in the Vector Block directly.  Also I'll
point out again that pulling the trigger locks out any changes to the
direction moved, allowing the image to bounce off the walls until the
trigger is released.  The crippled version "JX" removed that and would
lock out the joystick being returned to center so that it would bounce
around the screen forever.
Since the screen is blank until then and it looked like just a blank
screen, I updated it to draw one Green image without using the vector
draw routine, but needed to tell it there was something to erase when it
did the first move, so I had to set the vbBLNK bit and store the address
in vbOADD for it to use.
That first update was also when I added the Red whenever the trigger was
pulled, instead of always being Blue.

to BASIC, but they explain about the color boundary that can be set up for
eight colors for a cartridge.  The same idea applies to BASIC, but you have
less colors to work with.  In BASIC you have 2 colors per side of the boundary.
Without BASIC (in the cartridges) you have 4 colors per side of the boundary.

interrupts, then you can get more colors to display on the screen like some of
the games did (Hey, Brett!, care to chime in?).

I've seen this question come up quite a few times over the years.  Many people
think that the Astrocade can display 256 colors in BASIC.  BASIC, alone, can
never display 256 colors (it needs help from machine language subroutines to
do that).  So, for the most part remember these rules:

Bally or AstroBASIC - 2 colors OR 4 colors when using vertical color boundaries
Carts - 4 colors OR 8 colors when using vertical color boundaries

I can't think of any cartridge that doesn't use right colors in SOME way, but
there are quite a few BASIC games that are monochrome (as Bill has noticed).

The problem is timing.

Let's say that I draw a vertical bar in the center of the screen. It will be a solid color unless
I do something specific to change the color register.

I can...

Change it every VBL interrupt, then the entire box will change color over time.

Or I can...

Write a tight loop that changes the color register continuously, then the color of the box
will vary from top to bottom. (I did this for the splash screen for Treasure Cove and ICBM
Attack.)


As to the 2 color limitation of Basic, it is using 1 bit for screen memory lookup. The
cartridges used 2 bits giving 4 colors. I think the arcade version used 4 bits for 16 colors.

Why limit the screen memory to 2 colors? Well, in the arcade, screen memory and memory
are the same thing. If you want room to store programs and variables, you need to take 
memory from the screen.

The Maze game was a good example of this using the bottom of the screen as 'scratch
pad' memory for variables. The maze game took screen space, not screen depth.
The Basic cartridge takes screen depth, not screen space.

The reason for losing timing information for the recordings is KCS only extracts actual data information from the wav files. It seems it takes some time for the Astrocade to sort things up after loading/recording each program line, so there's some "blank space" between them. When converting wav files to prg this information is lost, and if you re-convert prg files to wav using the default program settings, you get a "turbo" recording, with zero delays. The Basic interpreter isn't fast enough to read the recordings without the delays, as I confirmed when I sent my first attempt at conversion to Paul, so I had to use an workaround: I instructed KCS to add a 50 ms delay after EACH program byte, and it seems it was good enough to load them without errors, though it isn't neither an optimal or safe threshold. I just didn't want to bother Paul with: "Did 50 ms worked? Yes? So, let's try 25. Not working? What about 37 ms?" and so on.

And Paul said there are programs that rely in such blank space (plain carrier tone without data) for timing. KCS is going to kill their timing information the same way I described above, so I think I going to develop some sort of program to keep such timing information when needed.

Additionally, with a greater understanding on Basic timing needs I could try to improve loading times for programs that don't rely on timing, but this would require either lots of tests using real hardware (not an option for me) or a thorough examination of the Basic loading routines, with focus on instruction timings (this would be a real pain, but it is possible).
